ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows two coordinate axes in the θ = π/2 plane. The horizontal axis can be taken as the x-axis, and the vertical axis can be taken as the y-axis. One antenna element is located in the positive direction of the vertical axis, at a distance s from the origin, that is, r1 = (0, s, 0); another antenna element is located in the positive direction of the horizontal axis, at a distance s from the origin, that is, r2 = (s, 0, 0). The figure also marks the azimuth angle φ, and φ = 0 corresponds to observing along the +x direction. Reasoning: According to the problem, the two identical elements are excited with equal amplitudes and differ by 180°, so the excitation weights can be taken as 1 and -1. For θ = π/2, φ = 0, the far-field observation direction unit vector is rhat = xhat, therefore rhat · r1 = 0, and rhat · r2 = s. After normalizing to the field strength of a single element, the array factor magnitude is |1 - exp(j k s)|. Where k = 2π/λ, so |1 - exp(jks)| = 2|sin(ks/2)| = 2|sin(πs/λ)|. According to the problem/common option convention, it is written as 2 sin(πs/λ).

method.method_draft: Assign coordinates from the figure: upper element \(r_1=(0,s,0)\), right element \(r_2=(s,0,0)\). For \(\theta=\pi/2,\phi=0\), take \(\hat r=\hat x\), giving \(\hat r\cdot r_1=0\) and \(\hat r\cdot r_2=s\). From the text, the two excitations have equal amplitudes and 180° polarity difference, so use weights \(1\) and \(-1\). The normalized resultant is \(|1-e^{jks}|\). With \(k=2\pi/\lambda\), simplify to \(2|\sin(ks/2)|=2\sin(\pi s/\lambda)\) under the usual stated magnitude/convention.
